---
title: "Dynamic AD-AS with a Taylor Rule"
subtitle: "How monetary policy stabilizes output and inflation — and when it fails"
---

{{< include ../_includes/generated/adassim-prereqs.md >}}

::: {.im-tldr}
**TL;DR** — Three equations (demand, supply, policy) generate joint output/inflation dynamics. An IS curve links the real interest rate to output; an expectations-augmented Phillips curve links the output gap to inflation; and a Taylor rule sets the interest rate in response to inflation. Whether the system settles down hinges on the **Taylor principle**: because spending responds to the *real* rate, the central bank must raise the *nominal* rate more than one-for-one with inflation (φπ > 1) for policy to tighten at all — which is what makes the dynamics self-correcting.
:::

## You'll be able to

- Trace how a Taylor-rule interest rate feeds through the IS curve into output, and then through the Phillips curve into inflation.
- Explain why φπ > 1 (the Taylor principle) is necessary for the inflation path to converge.
- Read a time-series chart of the dynamic AD-AS model and identify convergent versus oscillatory/divergent paths.

## Explore the model

::: {.im-sim-hero}
::: {.im-sim-label}
Drag a slider — the output, inflation, and interest-rate paths update live
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof pi_e    = Inputs.range([0, 5], {value: 3.0, step: 0.1, label: "initial inflation π₀"})
viewof pi_star = Inputs.range([0, 5], {value: 2.0, step: 0.1, label: "target inflation π*"})
viewof phi_pi  = Inputs.range([0, 3], {value: 1.5, step: 0.1, label: "Taylor coefficient φπ"})
viewof alpha   = Inputs.range([1, 10], {value: 5.0, step: 0.5, label: "IS sensitivity α"})
viewof lamb    = Inputs.range([0.05, 1], {value: 0.2, step: 0.05, label: "Phillips slope λ"})
viewof T       = Inputs.range([10, 60], {value: 25, step: 5, label: "periods T"})

sim = {
  // Taylor rule sets the NOMINAL rate; Fisher converts it to the real rate that
  // the IS curve responds to, with adaptive expectations πᵉ_t = π_{t−1}:
  //   i_t = r̄ + π* + φπ(π_{t−1} − π*),  r_t = i_t − πᵉ_t
  //       = r̄ + (φπ − 1)(π_{t−1} − π*)
  // Only φπ > 1 raises the REAL rate when inflation is high — the Taylor principle.
  const Ybar = 100, rbar = 2;
  const pi = [], Y = [], r = [], i = [];
  pi[0] = pi_e;
  i[0]  = rbar + pi_star + phi_pi * (pi[0] - pi_star);
  r[0]  = rbar + (phi_pi - 1) * (pi[0] - pi_star);
  Y[0]  = Ybar - alpha * (r[0] - rbar);
  for (let t = 1; t < T; t++) {
    i[t]  = rbar + pi_star + phi_pi * (pi[t-1] - pi_star);
    r[t]  = rbar + (phi_pi - 1) * (pi[t-1] - pi_star);
    Y[t]  = Ybar - alpha * (r[t] - rbar);
    pi[t] = pi[t-1] + lamb * (Y[t] - Ybar);
  }
  const rows = [];
  for (let t = 0; t < T; t++) {
    rows.push({t, value: pi[t],        series: "inflation π"});
    rows.push({t, value: Y[t] - Ybar,  series: "output gap (Y − Ȳ)"});
    rows.push({t, value: r[t],         series: "real interest rate r"});
  }
  return rows;
}

Plot.plot({
  marginLeft: 50, height: 340,
  color: {legend: true},
  x: {label: "time (periods) →"},
  y: {grid: true, label: "level / gap"},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "#cccccc"}),
    Plot.line(sim, {x: "t", y: "value", stroke: "series", strokeWidth: 2})
  ]
})
```

Watch what happens as you lower φπ below 1 — the Taylor principle fails and the paths stop converging.
:::

## Core intuition

The model has three moving parts that interact every period. The [Taylor rule]{.im-glossary-term} sets the central bank's *nominal* interest rate: if last period's inflation was above target, the bank raises rates. But spending responds to the *real* rate, and by the Fisher relation the real rate is the nominal rate minus expected inflation. That is the whole subtlety: raising the nominal rate one-for-one with inflation leaves the real rate *unchanged* and does nothing. Only a response steeper than one-for-one — φπ > 1, the [Taylor principle]{.im-glossary-term} — actually tightens in real terms. When it does, the higher real rate discourages spending through the IS curve, pulling output below potential and creating a negative [output gap]{.im-glossary-term}, and the negative gap pushes inflation down through the [expectations-augmented Phillips curve]{.im-glossary-term}. The loop is then self-correcting. Below φπ = 1 it runs in reverse: a burst of inflation *cuts* the real rate, demand strengthens, and inflation climbs further.

The key institutional detail is the **lag** in the Taylor rule: the central bank responds to *last period's* inflation, not this period's. This one-period delay is realistic (central banks observe lagged data) and is what gives the model its dynamic character — the economy cannot jump instantly to equilibrium.

::: {.im-math-toggle}
<details>
<summary>Show the math (full model + stability condition)</summary>

**Three equations, simulated period-by-period:**

Taylor rule — the central bank sets the *nominal* rate in response to *lagged* inflation:
$$i_t = \bar{r} + \pi^* + \varphi_\pi\,(\pi_{t-1} - \pi^*)$$

Fisher equation — spending responds to the *real* rate, and with adaptive expectations $\pi^e_t = \pi_{t-1}$:
$$r_t = i_t - \pi^e_t = \bar{r} + (\varphi_\pi - 1)\,(\pi_{t-1} - \pi^*)$$

IS curve (demand):
$$Y_t = \bar{Y} - \alpha\,(r_t - \bar{r})$$

Expectations-augmented Phillips curve (AS / supply):
$$\pi_t = \pi^e_t + \lambda\,(Y_t - \bar{Y}) = \pi_{t-1} + \lambda\,(Y_t - \bar{Y})$$

**Initial period** $t = 0$: set $\pi_0$ from the slider, then $r_0 = \bar{r} + (\varphi_\pi - 1)(\pi_0 - \pi^*)$ and $Y_0 = \bar{Y} - \alpha(r_0 - \bar{r})$.

**Parity check** (defaults: $\pi_0 = 3$, $\pi^* = 2$, $\bar{Y} = 100$, $\bar{r} = 2$, $\alpha = 5$, $\varphi_\pi = 1.5$, $\lambda = 0.2$):
$$r_0 = 2 + 0.5(3 - 2) = 2.5, \quad Y_0 = 100 - 5(2.5 - 2) = 97.5.$$
$$r_1 = 2.5, \quad Y_1 = 97.5, \quad \pi_1 = 3 + 0.2(97.5 - 100) = 2.5.$$

**Stability (the Taylor principle).** Substituting the Fisher-adjusted rule and the IS curve into the Phillips curve gives a first-order difference equation in the inflation gap $\tilde\pi_t = \pi_t - \pi^*$:
$$\tilde\pi_t = \bigl[1 - \lambda\alpha\,(\varphi_\pi - 1)\bigr]\,\tilde\pi_{t-1}.$$
For convergence the coefficient must have absolute value less than 1:
$$\bigl|1 - \lambda\alpha\,(\varphi_\pi - 1)\bigr| < 1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0 < \lambda\alpha\,(\varphi_\pi - 1) < 2.$$
The left inequality is the **Taylor principle**: it requires $\varphi_\pi > 1$, full stop. The reason is the Fisher equation. Spending responds to the *real* rate $r = i - \pi^e$, so when inflation rises by a point the nominal rate must rise by *more* than a point for the real rate to rise at all. At $\varphi_\pi < 1$ a burst of inflation actually *lowers* the real rate, stimulating demand and raising inflation further — the gap feeds on itself.

With the defaults $\lambda = 0.2$, $\alpha = 5$ (so $\lambda\alpha = 1$) the coefficient is simply $2 - \varphi_\pi$: convergence for $1 < \varphi_\pi < 3$, a knife-edge at $\varphi_\pi = 1$ (the gap neither grows nor shrinks) and at $\varphi_\pi = 3$ (permanent oscillation), and divergence outside. At the default $\varphi_\pi = 1.5$ the gap shrinks by half each period.

</details>
:::

## What the simulator showed

At the default φπ = 1.5 the three series settle down: inflation starts at π₀ = 3, one point above the π* = 2 target, and closes half the remaining gap every period — 3.0, 2.5, 2.25, 2.125, … — while the output gap and the real rate shrink toward zero alongside it. The economy starts out of equilibrium and the adjustment plays out over several periods; inflation does not jump to target instantly. Set π₀ = π* = 2 and nothing moves at all: the economy is already at rest.

Now lower φπ below 1 — try φπ = 0.5. The paths *diverge*: inflation climbs 3.0, 3.5, 4.25, 5.375, … and the output gap grows with it, because a nominal-rate response weaker than one-for-one lets the real rate *fall* as inflation rises. Set φπ = 1 exactly and the gap freezes at its initial value forever — the knife-edge. Push φπ to 2 and inflation snaps to target in a single period; push it to 3 and the correction overshoots so hard the economy oscillates permanently between 3 and 1. Stabilizing requires a response that is more than one-for-one, but not unboundedly aggressive.

## Shocks and adjustment

So far the economy was displaced from equilibrium only because expectations started away from target (πᵉ ≠ π\*). Real economies are also hit by **shocks** — sudden disturbances to demand or supply. The same three equations handle them: add a disturbance term ε^AD to the IS curve and ε^AS to the Phillips curve, and the model traces out an *impulse response* — the path of output and inflation back to the steady state after the shock hits.

The standard catalogue:

- **Demand shocks (ε^AD).** A drop in consumer confidence or government spending (ε^AD < 0) shifts AD left: output falls, and the negative output gap pulls inflation down with it. Output and inflation move in the **same direction**, so the Taylor rule faces no dilemma — cutting rates supports output *and* pushes inflation back toward target.
- **Supply shocks (ε^AS).** A rise in production costs — the classic case is an oil-price spike (ε^AS > 0) — shifts AS up: inflation rises while the policy response depresses output. Output and inflation move in **opposite directions**; this is the "stagflationary" case, and it confronts the central bank with a genuine dilemma: fighting inflation requires raising the rate, which deepens the output loss, while supporting output would let inflation run further above target. A favorable supply shock (ε^AS < 0, e.g. falling oil prices) is the mirror image: inflation falls and output rises.
- **Expectations shocks.** A sudden jump in initial inflation (or expected inflation) is exactly the configuration the first simulator starts from — πᵉ = 3 above π* = 2 — so you have already seen its impulse response above.

Shocks also differ in **persistence**. A one-off shock hits for a single period and then vanishes; a persistent shock decays gradually (here, geometrically at rate ρ). The more persistent the shock, the longer the Taylor rule must keep the interest rate away from its natural level, and the longer output and inflation stay displaced.

::: {.im-sim-hero}
::: {.im-sim-label}
Pick a shock — the impulse response of output and inflation updates live (it also responds to the φπ and T sliders above)
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof shock_kind = Inputs.radio(["demand", "supply"], {value: "demand", label: "shock type"})
viewof shock_size = Inputs.range([-8, 8], {value: -5, step: 0.5, label: "shock size ε"})
viewof shock_rho  = Inputs.range([0, 0.9], {value: 0, step: 0.05, label: "persistence ρ"})

shockSim = {
  // Same three equations as above (nominal Taylor rule + Fisher + adaptive
  // expectations), with the economy starting AT target so the shock is the only
  // disturbance, and flatter IS/Phillips slopes (λ·α = 0.3) so the impulse
  // responses decay gently enough to read across the whole φπ > 1 range.
  const YbarS = 100, rbarS = 2, piStarS = 2;
  const alphaS = 2, lambdaS = 0.15;
  const t0 = 2; // shock arrives in period 2
  const piS = [], YS = [], rS = [];
  piS[0] = piStarS;
  rS[0]  = rbarS + (phi_pi - 1) * (piS[0] - piStarS);
  YS[0]  = YbarS - alphaS * (rS[0] - rbarS);
  for (let t = 1; t < T; t++) {
    const eps = t >= t0 ? shock_size * Math.pow(shock_rho, t - t0) : 0;
    const eAD = shock_kind === "demand" ? eps : 0;
    const eAS = shock_kind === "supply" ? eps : 0;
    rS[t]  = rbarS + (phi_pi - 1) * (piS[t-1] - piStarS);
    YS[t]  = YbarS - alphaS * (rS[t] - rbarS) + eAD;
    piS[t] = piS[t-1] + lambdaS * (YS[t] - YbarS) + eAS;
  }
  const rows = [];
  for (let t = 0; t < T; t++) {
    rows.push({t, value: YS[t] - YbarS,   series: "output gap (Y − Ȳ)"});
    rows.push({t, value: piS[t] - piStarS, series: "inflation gap (π − π*)"});
  }
  return rows;
}

Plot.plot({
  marginLeft: 50, height: 320,
  color: {
    legend: true,
    domain: ["output gap (Y − Ȳ)", "inflation gap (π − π*)"],
    range: ["var(--im-accent)", "var(--im-warn)"]
  },
  x: {label: "time (periods) →"},
  y: {grid: true, label: "deviation from steady state"},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "var(--im-sim)", strokeDasharray: "4 4"}),
    Plot.ruleX([2], {stroke: "var(--im-fg-muted)", strokeDasharray: "2 4"}),
    Plot.line(shockSim, {x: "t", y: "value", stroke: "series", strokeWidth: 2})
  ]
})
```

The dashed red line is the steady state (zero gaps); the vertical dashed line marks the shock's arrival in period 2. Switch to a **supply** shock with ε = +5 — output and inflation now move in opposite directions.
:::

::: {.im-math-toggle}
<details>
<summary>Show the math (shock-augmented model)</summary>

The IS and Phillips curves gain disturbance terms; the policy block is unchanged:

$$Y_t = \bar{Y} - \alpha\,(r_t - \bar{r}) + \varepsilon^{AD}_t$$
$$\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \lambda\,(Y_t - \bar{Y}) + \varepsilon^{AS}_t$$
$$r_t = \bar{r} + (\varphi_\pi - 1)\,(\pi_{t-1} - \pi^*)$$

The shock arrives in period $t_0 = 2$ with size $\varepsilon$ and decays geometrically at rate $\rho$:
$$\varepsilon_t = \varepsilon\,\rho^{\,t - t_0} \quad \text{for } t \ge t_0, \qquad \varepsilon_t = 0 \text{ before.}$$
$\rho = 0$ is a one-off shock; $\rho$ close to 1 is a persistent one.

**Local calibration.** This simulator starts the economy *at* target ($\pi_0 = \pi^* = 2$) so the impulse response isolates the shock, and uses flatter slopes $\alpha = 2$, $\lambda = 0.15$. The feedback coefficient is $1 - 0.3(\varphi_\pi - 1)$, which is inside $(-1, 1)$ for every $\varphi_\pi > 1$ on the slider — so with the Taylor principle satisfied the responses always decay back to steady state, gently at $\varphi_\pi$ just above 1 and fastest near $\varphi_\pi = 3$. Drop $\varphi_\pi$ below 1 and even a one-off shock never dies out, the same failure the first simulator shows.

**Reading the responses.** A demand shock moves output on impact and inflation with it ($\lambda \varepsilon^{AD}$ in the same direction). A supply shock moves inflation on impact while output is untouched *in the impact period*; the output loss arrives one period later, when the Taylor rule reacts to the higher inflation — the policy response, not the shock itself, is what depresses output.

</details>
:::

## Common confusions

::: {.im-confusion}
**"The central bank can hit the target instantly."** No — the Taylor rule responds to *lagged* inflation, so even perfect policy (φπ > 1) takes several periods of adjustment before inflation reaches its long-run level. The one-period lag is baked into the model structure and reflects real-world data lags and policy transmission delays.
:::

::: {.im-confusion}
**"Any positive φπ stabilizes the economy."** No — the Taylor principle requires φπ > 1, and the reason is the Fisher equation. If the bank raises the *nominal* rate by less than one point for each point of excess inflation, the *real* rate — which is what spending responds to — actually **falls**. Policy is then loosening exactly when it should tighten, so inflation gaps become self-reinforcing and the economy diverges. Note the other end too: with λα = 1 the response can also be *too* aggressive (φπ ≥ 3 here), overshooting into permanent oscillation. Stability needs 1 < φπ < 3.
:::

::: {.im-confusion}
**"Demand and supply shocks look the same in the data."** No — the co-movement of output and inflation identifies them. Under a demand shock the two move in the *same* direction (a slump lowers both); under a supply shock they move in *opposite* directions (an oil-price spike raises inflation while output falls — stagflation). This is also why the policy problem differs: a demand shock lets the Taylor rule fight both gaps with one instrument, while a supply shock forces a trade-off between them.
:::

## Self-check

<div class="im-mcq">
<div class="im-q-label">Q1 · concept</div>

What does the Taylor principle require, and why does it matter for stability?

<details><summary>a\) φπ > 0 — any positive response to inflation is stabilizing</summary>
No — a positive response is necessary but not sufficient. If φπ < 1 the central bank raises rates by less than the inflation gap, leaving the real interest rate adjustment too small to close the gap. Inflation deviations feed on themselves.
</details>
<details><summary>b\) φπ > 1 — the rate response must exceed the inflation gap one-for-one</summary>
**Correct**. Spending responds to the real rate $r = i - \pi^e$, so only a *more*-than-proportionate nominal hike actually raises the real rate. When it does, output falls via the IS curve and inflation falls via the Phillips curve — a self-correcting loop. Below 1 the real rate moves the wrong way and the loop amplifies rather than dampens.
</details>
<details><summary>c\) φπ = 1 exactly — the rate response must match inflation one-for-one</summary>
No — at φπ = 1 the economy is on the boundary: the nominal rate moves one-for-one with inflation, so by the Fisher relation the *real* rate never moves, the feedback coefficient equals 1, and the inflation gap neither grows nor shrinks. You need the strict inequality φπ > 1 for convergence.
</details>
</div>

<div class="im-mcq">
<div class="im-q-label">Q2 · simulator challenge</div>

Set φπ = 0.5 in the simulator (keep all other defaults: π₀ = 3, π* = 2, α = 5, λ = 0.2, T = 25). Describe what happens to the inflation path, and say what the real interest rate is doing.

<details><summary>Reveal answer</summary>
The Taylor principle is violated, and inflation **diverges**: 3.0, 3.5, 4.25, 5.375, 7.06, … growing by half the gap each period (the coefficient is $1 - \lambda\alpha(\varphi_\pi-1) = 1.5$). Watch the real-rate series to see why — with φπ = 0.5, inflation *above* target pushes the real rate *below* $\bar r$, so policy stimulates an already-overheating economy. Contrast φπ = 1.5, where the same gap shrinks by half each period and the real rate rises above $\bar r$ exactly when inflation is high.
</details>
</div>
